extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (indie and trad), authors considering publishing strategy, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, market-focused advice for fiction writers about story quality, pricing, format choices, and adapting to technological change in publishing. Emphasizes what readers want and how authors can position their work in a shifting market.

rubrics_metrics.name: People want good stories
rubrics_metrics.description: People are still going to want good stories to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A self-publishing author has to be good, not just prolific. Quality writing from a human being is the best way to find a loyal readership. This is being tested as AI makes it possible to churn out dozens of 'novels' a year of mediocre quality; human-quality works will stand out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price expectations — readers won’t pay as much
rubrics_metrics.description: They’re not going to pay as much money to get them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Big publishers feared inexpensive ebooks would erode hardcover sales. In practice hardcovers still sell for brand names, trade paper sells more, and many readers seek the best deals. Indie authors selling at $2.99–$5.99 occupy the current 'sweet spot' for pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interruptive added digital content
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers prefer to get caught up in a story without pausing to find or endure added 'stuff.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to embed extra digital content (links, YouTube, other media — e.g., 'Vooks') largely did not take off. Authors should avoid relying on extraneous digital features that break immersion; readers want an uninterrupted reading experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider format resilience and platform compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Print has proved resilient; many readers remain 'paper people'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical books continue to sell; hardcovers sell especially for established/brand-name authors, and trade paper remains popular. Also note technical limits: embedded links and some digital features may work on phones but not on devices like Kindle, so choose formats and features with platform compatibility in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author brand and craft matter for higher-format sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardcovers still sell (if they are by 'brand names').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To command premium formats and prices, authors need a recognizable brand and strong craft. For indie authors, focusing on quality and building readership is a pathway to higher-format sales and long-term career viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality over gimmick or high output
rubrics_metrics.description: Being prolific alone isn’t sufficient if work is mediocre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The market (and now AI) makes high-volume, low-quality output possible; however, sustained reader loyalty depends on well-crafted stories. Don’t rely on novelty formats or volume alone to build a career — invest in quality writing and storytelling craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be adaptable to rapid technological change
rubrics_metrics.description: The pace of change in publishing and tech is rapid and produces anxiety among creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major developments (e.g., Kindle, AI advances) can rapidly alter publishing paradigms. Authors should watch trends, be ready to adapt strategy (pricing, format, distribution), but focus on fundamentals — strong stories and reader relationships — that endure through change.
